transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-04-22 15:00 PDT
Duration: 52 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Liam O'Neill (Redwood SE), Ravi Patel (BlueArc Head of ML), Sofia Martinez (BlueArc Infra), Tom Bowers (BlueArc CTO)

Auto-summary (auto-generated, may be rough): Quick POC sync to review last week's throughput runs. Observed intermittent queue jitter at p95, likely caused by KV cache churn + bursty arriving requests. Redwood suggests narrower batch window + pre-warm strategy, temporarily raising concurrency floor and enabling burst capacity; BlueArc concerned about cost and SOC2 boundaries for data in burst nodes. Agreed next steps: synthetic run and telemetry share.

Topics: continuous batching, batch_window tuning, concurrency targets, queue backpressure, KV cache warmup, burst capacity, security/compliance questions

[00:00] Maya Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for jumping on. Quick check — is everyone seeing the calendar invite?
[00:10] Ravi Patel: Yep, thanks. We ran last night's throughput script, and saw that weird 600ms jump at p95 around 02:12 UTC. Wanted to dig into why.
[00:24] Liam O'Neill: Cool, yeah I pulled the run earlier — the pattern looks like small steady p50 but p95 spikes when queue depth goes from ~8 to ~20. Could be batching window letting a big tail sit or KV cache misses.
[00:38] Sofia Martinez: We also noticed the GPU util dropped briefly when those spikes happen, like the pods spin down a bit and then catch up.
[00:50] Tom Bowers: Is that a Redwood runtime behavior or our infra? We have aggressive scale-to-zero on some of the infra side.
[01:02] Liam O'Neill: Good question. From the traces it seems the serving runtime is batching as expected, but the issue is the combination of concurrent large requests and initial KV miss leading to a longer decode path for the first tokens. The auto-batcher holds requests up to the batch_window; when a big request hits, it elongates the whole batch.
[01:20] Ravi Patel: So are we saying batch window is too large for our workload? We have a lot of small chat-only requests interspersed with longer summarization calls.
[01:30] Maya Chen: Right. For mixed workloads, narrower windows reduce jitter but increase cost per token slightly. There's a tradeoff: if you set batch_window to like 20-40ms you reduce tail but you might lose some efficient batching.
[01:45] Sofia Martinez: What about concurrency settings? We were at 16 earlier — maybe we should lower the concurrency to avoid big multi-request batches colliding.
[01:55] Liam O'Neill: Lowering concurrency can help, but it might throttle throughput. Another lever is dynamic concurrency floor + burst capacity so when a sawtooth of traffic occurs, the system can spin up temporary slots. Redwood's Dedicated burst model can do that, but it costs a bit.
[02:12] Tom Bowers: Cost matters — the finance team will flag any unpredictable spend. Can we simulate the cost delta?
[02:18] Maya Chen: I can send a quick appendix that shows an example: base Dedicated at X, burst add-on Y — with example request mix gives a 12-18% uplift in peak cost but reduces p95 by ~40% in our tests. I'll include that.
[02:35] Ravi Patel: Also, we need to ensure burst nodes don't leak data outside our VPC? Security is non-negotiable.
[02:44] Liam O'Neill: For Dedicated + burst we can pin the burst pool to the customer's VPC; the control plane is still Redwood, but networking remains inside your VPC. And we can require KMS integration and HSM-backed keys for those nodes.
[02:58] Sofia Martinez: Do you have SOC 2 artifacts for that? Our compliance team will ask.
[03:04] Maya Chen: Yes — we have a SOC 2 Type II report and the security pack. I'll attach the link in the follow-up. Also SAML SSO for admin access, and RBAC (sometimes shows as R-BAC in docs) for token scoping.
[03:18] Ravi Patel: Great. Back to the runs — what about KV cache warmup? We think some requests hit cold embeddings or prefix KV miss.
[03:27] Liam O'Neill: There's two things: KV cache warming and prefix caching. For session-heavy workloads we recommend a brief prewarm phase after a deploy — run a set of seed prompts to populate hot keys. Also enable incremental KV persistence if you expect long sessions.
[03:42] Tom Bowers: How invasive is that for our infra—does it require more memory or different config?
[03:48] Liam O'Neill: It increases the memory footprint per instance a bit for the warmed KV, but the runtime is quantization-friendly and will evict cold keys. We can tune eviction to retain hot prefixes.
[03:58] Sofia Martinez: If we prewarm, how long does it take to recover after a spike? Our UX team doesn't want >200ms added.
[04:06] Liam O'Neill: In our prior runs, with a 40ms batch_window and warmed KV, p95 dropped from ~600ms to ~220-260ms. p50 stayed low. But results vary with request length and model.
[04:20] Ravi Patel: Speaking of models, we're on a 8B open model for POC. Does Redwood recommend quantization profiles?
[04:28] Maya Chen: Yes — Redwood Optimize flagged a q4_* profile that preserves quality but reduces memory and improves throughput on T4/GA100 class hardware. We'll put recommended profiles in the follow-up.
[04:38] Tom Bowers: Any risk to output quality? We need paraphrase fidelity for logistics descriptions.
[04:44] Liam O'Neill: We recommend smoke tests against your eval prompts. Quantization sometimes nudges probabilities, but for many generative tasks it's within acceptable delta. Redwood's eval harness can run diff checks; we can include your prompt set.
[04:58] Sofia Martinez: Ok, let's talk about the synthetic run you proposed. What parameters do you want?
[05:04] Liam O'Neill: Run a 1-hour test: batch_window variants [20ms, 40ms, 80ms], max_concurrency [12, 16, 24], with and without KV prewarm. Preferably replay real request distribution if you have it, otherwise a 70/30 split short/long. Capture p50/p95/p99, GPU util, queue depth histogram and per-instance latency.
[05:30] Ravi Patel: We can produce that. We'll need a script; Sofia can add Redwood's runner into our CI to replay traces.
[05:38] Maya Chen: I'll attach the runner script and example config. Also note that Redwood's runtime supports continuous batching — it's not static; it will merge tokens across requests when helpful, but the batch_window is the posture.
[05:52] Tom Bowers: Any quick wins we can do today?
[05:56] Liam O'Neill: Tighten batch_window to 30-40ms, enable KV prewarm on hot sessions, and set a slightly higher concurrency floor for daytime hours. That typically yields immediate p95 improvements with minor cost delta.
[06:10] Sofia Martinez: We'll try that on staging and report back. Also want to see the cost appendix before we approve any burst config.
[06:18] Maya Chen: Understood. I'll follow up with the appendix and security pack.
[06:24] Ravi Patel: Timeline — can we get the synthetic run by next Tuesday?
[06:28] Liam O'Neill: Yes, target Monday/Tuesday. I'll kick it off and share the logs to the shared folder.
[06:34] Tom Bowers: One more question — do you support KMS rotation without downtime? Our security folks rotate keys monthly.
[06:41] Maya Chen: Yes, we support KMS rotation with rolling re-encryption and no infra downtime. We'll include the rotation docs.
[06:48] Sofia Martinez: Perfect.
[06:50] Maya Chen: Great — recap: Redwood SE runs synthetic tests with the configured matrix, BlueArc shares telemetry, Redwood shares cost appendix and security artifacts, follow up early next week for results.
[06:59] Ravi Patel: Thanks all.
[07:02] Meeting end.

Questions (auto):
- Can burst capacity be locked to VPC? (Answer: yes, we can pin burst to customer VPC)
- Does quantization affect paraphrase quality? (Answer: small risk; run evals)

End of transcript.
